Maximum likelihood estimation of \(\theta\) and \(\sigma\) based on Pitman sampling formula

Source: R/estimation.R
optim_pitman.Rd

optim_pitman() computes the maximum likelihood estimate of Pitman \((\theta,\sigma)\) parameters for a given species abundance distribution \((n_1, ..., n_k)\) where \(n_i\) is the number of organisms of species i in the sample and k is the total number of species (for all \(i, n_i > 0\)). The input should be a vector and initial values of \((\theta,\sigma)\) can be supplied with the argument init_vals = c(theta_init, sigma_init) with the condition theta_init > 0 and 0 < sigma_init < 1.

The log-likelihood function is maximised with the box-constrained quasi-Newton method L-BFGS-B (stats::optim()) using the exact gradient, on the scale \((\log\theta,\sigma)\). The optimisation is run from init_vals and from a second starting point derived from the Ewens estimate, and the better result is kept.

Usage

optim_pitman(
  input_abundances,
  init_vals = c(10, 0.1),
  lower = c(1e-06, 1e-08),
  upper = NULL
)

Arguments

input_abundances

a vector of integers (species abundances); species with zero abundance are ignored

init_vals

initial values of (theta, sigma), a vector of two real numbers

lower, upper

bounds of the search interval for c(theta, sigma)

Value

A list with

theta

parameter \(\theta\), a real value

sigma

parameter \(\sigma\), a real value

logl

maximal log-likelihood (log-probability of the partition, see optim_ewens()), a real value; it is comparable with the logl value of optim_ewens()

converged

TRUE if the optimiser reported convergence

Search interval and boundary warnings

By default \(\theta\) is searched in [1e-6, J] and \(\sigma\) in [1e-8, 1 - 1e-8], where J is the number of individuals. A warning is issued if an estimate lies on the edge of its interval (the likelihood then has no interior maximum, or the interval is too narrow); use lower and upper to change it.

See also

optim_ewens(), optim_multideme()

Examples

optim_pitman(c(234, 87, 34, 5, 4, 3, 3, 2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1), c(10.0, 0.1))
#> $theta
#> [1] 0.7110667
#> 
#> $sigma
#> [1] 0.2781073
#> 
#> $logl
#> [1] -432.4741
#> 
#> $converged
#> [1] TRUE
#>
